topics.title: Client relationship and fees
topics.intro: Chapter 4 of the Rules Regulating The Florida Bar tracks the ABA Model Rules in structure but is stricter on fees. Florida tests its contingent-fee rule heavily: the signed writing, the Statement of Client's Rights, the three-business-day cancellation right, the personal-injury fee schedule, and the 75/25 limit on dividing a fee with a referring lawyer.

rules.title: Allocation of authority and limited-scope representation
rules.rule: The client decides the objectives of the representation, including whether to settle, and in a criminal case whether to plead, waive a jury, and testify; the lawyer, after consulting the client, decides the means. A lawyer may limit the scope of a representation if the limitation is reasonable and the client gives informed consent in writing, and must not counsel or assist a client in conduct the lawyer knows is criminal or fraudulent.
rules.tip: A lawyer may discuss the legal consequences of any proposed course of conduct and help a client determine the validity, scope or meaning of the law; explaining is not assisting.
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 1.2(c) requires only informed consent to a limited-scope representation; Florida's rule requires that consent to be in writing.

rules.title: Competence, diligence and communication
rules.rule: A lawyer must provide competent representation, which requires the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary, including keeping abreast of the benefits and risks of relevant technology. A lawyer must act with reasonable diligence and promptness, keep the client reasonably informed, promptly comply with reasonable requests for information, and promptly tell the client about matters requiring the client's informed consent, such as a settlement offer.
rules.tip: A lawyer may take a matter outside his or her experience by studying it or associating with a competent lawyer. Failing to convey a settlement offer is a classic 4-1.4 violation even if the lawyer thinks the offer is too low.

rules.title: Clearly excessive fees and the basis of the fee
rules.rule: A lawyer may not enter into an agreement for, charge or collect an illegal, prohibited or clearly excessive fee or cost, or a fee generated by employment obtained through advertising or solicitation that violates the Rules. A fee is clearly excessive when, after a review of the facts, a lawyer of ordinary prudence would be left with a definite and firm conviction that it exceeds a reasonable fee, or when it is sought or secured by intentional misrepresentation or fraud upon the client, a nonclient party or a court.
elements: Reasonableness factors include the time, labor, novelty and skill required; the fee customarily charged locally; the amount involved and results obtained; time limits; the nature and length of the relationship; the lawyer's experience and reputation; and whether the fee is fixed or contingent

When the lawyer has not regularly represented the client, the basis or rate of the fee and costs must be communicated, preferably in writing, before or within a reasonable time after starting the representation
A fee that is nonrefundable in any part must be confirmed in writing explaining the parties' intent as to its nature and amount
rules.split: The ABA standard is an 'unreasonable' fee; Florida's disciplinary standard is a 'clearly excessive' fee, defined by the ordinary-prudent-lawyer test, and Florida separately bars collecting fees from employment obtained by improper advertising or solicitation.

rules.title: Contingent fees: the writing, prohibited cases and the closing statement
rules.rule: A contingent fee arrangement must be reduced to a written contract signed by the client and by a lawyer for each participating lawyer or firm, stating the method by which the fee is determined, and the client must receive a copy. No lawyer or firm may participate in the fee without the client's written consent, and each participating firm must sign and assume joint legal responsibility to the client. At the conclusion of the matter the lawyer must prepare a closing statement showing the outcome and the method of distribution, signed by the client and each participating lawyer.
exceptions: A lawyer may not charge a fee in a domestic relations matter contingent on securing a divorce or on the amount of alimony, support or a property settlement
A lawyer may not charge a contingent fee for representing a defendant in a criminal case
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 1.5(c) requires a writing signed by the client; Florida also requires the lawyer's signature (one for each participating firm) and joint responsibility for every firm sharing the fee.

rules.title: Personal-injury contingent fees: client's rights and the fee schedule
rules.rule: In personal injury, wrongful death and similar tort claims, the client must, before signing, receive, read and sign the Statement of Client's Rights, and the contract must let the client cancel by written notice within three business days of signing without owing any fee (though the lawyer may recover costs advanced). Any fee above the schedule in the rule is presumed clearly excessive unless approved in advance by the court.
elements: Before an answer is filed or arbitrators are demanded (or the time to answer expires): 33 1/3% of the first $1 million, 30% of the next $1 million, 20% of any amount over $2 million
After that point through judgment: 40% of the first $1 million, 30% of the next $1 million, 20% of any amount over $2 million
If all defendants admit liability in their answers and request trial only on damages: 33 1/3% of the first $1 million, 20% of the next $1 million, 15% of any amount over $2 million
An additional 5% of the recovery is allowed once an appeal is filed or post-judgment collection proceedings are required
exceptions: In medical liability cases, Art. I, § 26 of the Florida Constitution entitles the claimant to at least 70% of the first $250,000 of damages and 90% of damages above $250,000, exclusive of reasonable and customary costs; the rule sets out a specific procedure by which a client may knowingly waive that protection
rules.trap: The 33 1/3% tier ends when an answer is filed (or arbitration demanded), not when the lawyer files suit.
rules.authority: R. Regulating Fla. Bar 4-1.5(f)(4); Art. I, § 26, Fla. Const.

rules.title: Dividing fees between firms and referral fees
rules.rule: Lawyers in different firms may divide a fee only if the total fee is not clearly excessive and either the division is in proportion to the services each performs, or, by written agreement with the client, each lawyer assumes joint legal responsibility for the representation and agrees to be available for consultation with the client. In personal-injury contingent-fee cases, the lawyer with primary responsibility must receive at least 75% of the total fee and the lawyer with secondary responsibility no more than 25%; a share above 25% is presumed clearly excessive unless both lawyers accept substantially equal active participation and the court authorizes the larger division.
exceptions: The 25% limit does not apply where two or more firms accept substantially equal active participation, but the division must then be authorized by the court
rules.trap: A pure referral fee with no work is allowed in Florida only with written client consent and the referring lawyer's assumption of joint legal responsibility; in a PI contingency case it is also capped at 25% of the total fee.
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 1.5(e) allows a joint-responsibility division with client consent confirmed in writing but has no percentage cap; Florida's 75/25 rule for personal-injury cases is unique.

rules.title: Declining, withdrawing and protecting the client on exit
rules.rule: A lawyer must decline or withdraw if the representation will result in a violation of the Rules or other law, if the lawyer's physical or mental condition materially impairs the representation, if the lawyer is discharged, or if the client persists in a course of action involving the lawyer's services that the lawyer reasonably believes is criminal or fraudulent, or has used the lawyer's services to commit a crime or fraud, unless the client agrees to disclose and rectify it. A lawyer may withdraw for other reasons, such as when withdrawal can be done without material adverse effect on the client, the client insists on action the lawyer considers repugnant or imprudent, or the client fails substantially to pay after warning, but must obtain the tribunal's permission when its rules require it and must continue if ordered to do so.
elements: On termination, give reasonable notice, allow time to obtain other counsel, surrender papers and property the client is entitled to, and refund any unearned advance fee or expense
The lawyer may retain papers only to the extent other law (such as a valid lien) permits
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 1.16(b)(2)–(3) treats a client's persistence in crime or fraud involving the lawyer's services, or past use of those services for a crime or fraud, as grounds for permissive withdrawal. Florida's Rule 4-1.16(a)(4)–(5) makes withdrawal mandatory in both situations unless the client agrees to disclose and rectify the crime or fraud.
rules.trap: A client may discharge a lawyer at any time, with or without cause. A lawyer discharged without cause from a contingent-fee case recovers the reasonable value of services (quantum meruit), capped by the contract fee and payable only if the contingency occurs; the lawyer cannot insist on continuing.
rules.authority: R. Regulating Fla. Bar 4-1.16(a)–(d); Rosenberg v. Levin, 409 So. 2d 1016 (Fla. 1982)

topics.title: Trust accounts (Chapter 5)
topics.intro: Chapter 5 of the Rules Regulating The Florida Bar sets out the trust-accounting duties that ABA Model Rule 1.15 covers in a single rule, with far more detail. Misuse of trust money is among the most serious offenses a Florida lawyer can commit; essay questions typically involve a settlement check, a disputed fee, a medical provider's claim, or an advance fee deposit.

rules.title: What is trust money and where it goes
rules.rule: Money or other property entrusted to a lawyer for a specific purpose, including advances for fees, costs and expenses, is held in trust and may be applied only to that purpose. It must be kept in a separate account clearly labeled as a trust account, maintained in the state where the lawyer practices (or elsewhere with the client's consent), and kept separate from the lawyer's own property.
exceptions: The rule does not prevent a lawyer from retaining money on which the lawyer holds a valid lien for services, or from paying agreed fees out of the proceeds of transactions or collections
rules.trap: Client funds in the lawyer's possession are not subject to setoff or counterclaim for the lawyer's fees, and refusing to account for and deliver them on demand is treated as conversion. A lawyer cannot quietly apply one matter's trust money to an unpaid bill on another matter.

rules.title: No commingling
rules.rule: A lawyer may not commingle personal or firm funds with trust funds, except that the lawyer may keep in the trust account only enough of the lawyer's own money to cover bank service charges on the account. Fees the lawyer has earned must be withdrawn within a reasonable time after they become due unless the client disputes them.
rules.trap: Leaving earned fees in the trust account as a 'cushion' is commingling, and paying personal or office expenses directly from trust is misuse even if the lawyer has enough earned money in the account to cover it.
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 1.15(b) contains the same bank-charge exception; Florida's Chapter 5 adds detailed recordkeeping and procedural requirements around it.

rules.title: Advance fees versus true retainers
rules.rule: An advance payment for fees or costs not yet earned or incurred belongs to the client and must be placed in the trust account, then withdrawn only as the fees are earned or the costs incurred. A true retainer paid solely to secure the lawyer's availability, and a fee that is properly nonrefundable under a written agreement, is earned on receipt and should not be placed in trust.
rules.trap: Calling a payment a 'retainer' does not make it the lawyer's money. If it pays for future work, it is an advance fee held in trust, and any unearned portion must be refunded on termination.

rules.title: Notice, prompt delivery and disputed funds
rules.rule: On receiving funds or property in which a client or third person has an interest, the lawyer must promptly notify that person, promptly deliver what that person is entitled to receive, and on request render a full accounting. When two or more persons (one of whom may be the lawyer) claim an interest, the lawyer must keep the disputed portion in trust until the dispute is resolved and promptly distribute all undisputed portions.
elements: Third persons with a matured legal or equitable claim to the funds, such as a medical provider holding a letter of protection or a statutory lien, are protected; the lawyer may not simply hand the money to the client
If the dispute cannot be resolved, the lawyer may seek a court determination, such as by interpleader
rules.trap: A fee dispute justifies holding only the disputed amount, not the client's entire recovery.

rules.title: IOTA accounts
rules.rule: Nominal or short-term client funds, meaning funds that could not earn income for the client in excess of the cost of earning it, must be deposited in an interest-bearing IOTA account whose interest is paid to The Florida Bar Foundation. Funds that can earn net income for the client must instead be placed in a separate interest-bearing trust account for that client's benefit.
elements: The lawyer decides in good faith, considering the amount, how long the funds will be held, the rates available, and the cost of administering a separate account
The lawyer does not earn or keep any interest on client funds
rules.trap: Putting a large sum that will be held for a year into the pooled IOTA account deprives the client of interest the client could have earned and violates the rule.

rules.title: Records, reconciliations and sanctions
rules.rule: A lawyer must keep minimum trust accounting records, including deposit records, cancelled checks or their equivalent, bank statements, and a separate ledger for each client or matter, and must retain them for at least six years. The lawyer must reconcile the trust account at least monthly, must also compare the reconciled balance with the total of the individual client ledgers, and is responsible for trust-account compliance even when a nonlawyer employee keeps the books.
rules.tip: On an essay, misappropriation of client funds, even if the lawyer intended to repay, is usually treated as warranting disbarment absent strong mitigation.
rules.trap: Delegating bookkeeping to staff does not delegate responsibility; failure to supervise the person who embezzled from trust is itself a violation.

topics.title: Confidentiality and conflicts
topics.intro: Florida's confidentiality rule is the biggest departure from the ABA Model Rules: a Florida lawyer must reveal confidential information to the extent reasonably necessary to prevent a client from committing any crime, or to prevent death or substantial bodily harm. The conflict rules follow the Model Rules closely, with a few Florida twists such as the related-lawyers rule, the insured-client statement, and a separate rule on sexual conduct with clients.

rules.title: Scope of the duty of confidentiality
rules.rule: A lawyer must not reveal information relating to the representation of a client unless the client gives informed consent or an exception applies. The duty covers all information relating to the representation, whatever its source, and continues after the representation ends.
rules.trap: Confidentiality is broader than the attorney-client privilege. The evidentiary privilege protects only confidential lawyer-client communications from compelled disclosure; the ethical duty covers everything the lawyer learns in the representation, including public information and facts learned from third parties.
rules.authority: R. Regulating Fla. Bar 4-1.6(a); Fla. Stat. § 90.502

rules.title: When a Florida lawyer must reveal
rules.rule: A lawyer must reveal confidential information to the extent the lawyer reasonably believes necessary to prevent a client from committing a crime, or to prevent a death or substantial bodily harm to another.
rules.tip: The duty is forward-looking: it applies to a crime the client is about to commit, not to a crime already completed. A client's confession to a past crime stays confidential.
rules.trap: Students trained on the Model Rules answer 'may reveal.' In Florida, disclosure to prevent a client's crime, or to prevent death or substantial bodily harm, is mandatory.
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 1.6(b) makes all disclosures permissive ('may reveal'), and its financial-harm exceptions are limited to crimes or frauds in which the client used the lawyer's services. Florida requires disclosure to prevent any client crime and to prevent death or substantial bodily harm.

rules.title: When a Florida lawyer may reveal
rules.rule: A lawyer may reveal confidential information to the extent the lawyer reasonably believes necessary to serve the client's interest (unless the client has specifically told the lawyer not to), to establish a claim or defense in a controversy between lawyer and client, to defend against a criminal charge or civil claim based on conduct in which the client was involved, to respond to allegations about the lawyer's representation of the client, to comply with the Rules Regulating The Florida Bar, or to detect and resolve conflicts arising from a change of employment.
elements: Disclose no more than the lawyer reasonably believes necessary
When a court orders disclosure, the lawyer should assert legitimate objections and may comply once appeals are exhausted or not pursued

rules.title: Concurrent conflicts of interest
rules.rule: A concurrent conflict exists if the representation of one client will be directly adverse to another client, or if there is a substantial risk that the representation of one or more clients will be materially limited by the lawyer's responsibilities to another client, a former client, a third person, or the lawyer's own interest. The lawyer may proceed only if the lawyer reasonably believes he or she can provide competent and diligent representation to each client, the representation is not prohibited by law, it does not involve asserting a claim by one client against another in the same proceeding, and each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing or clearly stated on the record at a hearing.
exceptions: In common representation of multiple clients in one matter, the lawyer must explain the implications, advantages and risks of the joint representation

A lawyer related to another lawyer as parent, child, sibling or spouse may not represent a client directly adverse to a person the lawyer knows is represented by the relative, unless the client consents after consultation about the relationship
rules.tip: When the client is an organization, the lawyer represents the entity acting through its authorized constituents, not its officers or shareholders individually (Rule 4-1.13).
rules.split: Florida retains the related-lawyers conflict rule in 4-1.7(d); the ABA Model Rules no longer contain a separate rule on lawyers related by blood or marriage.

rules.title: Specific prohibited transactions
rules.rule: Rule 4-1.8 regulates particular lawyer-client dealings. A business transaction with a client is allowed only if the terms are fair and reasonable and fully disclosed in writing, the client is advised in writing to seek independent counsel and given a reasonable opportunity to do so, and the client gives informed consent in a writing signed by the client to the essential terms and the lawyer's role.
elements: Gifts: a lawyer may not solicit a substantial gift from a client or prepare an instrument giving the lawyer or a relative a substantial gift, unless the lawyer is related to the client
Literary or media rights: no agreement for them before the representation ends

Financial assistance: a lawyer may advance court costs and litigation expenses (repayment may depend on the outcome) and may pay them for an indigent client, but may not otherwise give financial assistance in pending or contemplated litigation
Aggregate settlements of claims for multiple clients require each client's informed consent in a signed writing

No agreement prospectively limiting malpractice liability unless the client is independently represented; settling a malpractice claim with an unrepresented client requires written advice to seek independent counsel
No proprietary interest in the cause of action except a lien authorized by law and a reasonable contingent fee
When an insurer pays the lawyer to defend its insured, Florida requires the lawyer to give the insured client a statement of the insured client's rights

rules.title: Sexual conduct with a client
rules.rule: Florida treats it as misconduct for a lawyer to engage in sexual conduct with a client or a client's representative that exploits or adversely affects the interests of the client or the lawyer-client relationship. The rule lists examples of prohibited conduct.
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 1.8(j) flatly bars sexual relations with a client unless a consensual sexual relationship existed before the representation began. Florida's rule, found in its misconduct rule rather than its conflicts rule, focuses on exploitation or harm to the client or the representation.
rules.trap: Do not cite a Florida 4-1.8(j) for this point; Florida's 4-1.8(j) concerns representation of insureds.
elements: Requiring or demanding sexual relations as a condition of the representation
Using coercion, intimidation or undue influence to begin sexual relations with a client
Continuing the representation when the sexual relationship causes the lawyer to render incompetent representation

rules.title: Former clients
rules.rule: A lawyer who formerly represented a client in a matter may not afterward represent another person in the same or a substantially related matter in which that person's interests are materially adverse to the former client, unless the former client gives informed consent. The lawyer also may not use information relating to the former representation to the former client's disadvantage unless the rules permit or the information has become generally known, and may not reveal it except as the rules permit.
rules.tip: Matters are substantially related if they involve the same transaction or legal dispute, or if there is a substantial risk that confidential factual information normally obtained in the prior matter would materially advance the new client's position.

rules.title: Imputation, lateral hires and prospective clients
rules.rule: While lawyers are associated in a firm, none may knowingly represent a client when any one of them practicing alone would be prohibited by Rule 4-1.7 or 4-1.9, unless the conflict rests on a personal interest of the disqualified lawyer that does not present a significant risk of limiting the others' representation. When a lawyer joins a new firm, the firm is disqualified from a matter that is the same as or substantially related to one in which the lawyer (or the old firm) represented an adverse client only if the lawyer actually acquired confidential information material to the matter.
exceptions: Former government lawyers and former judges, arbitrators and mediators may be screened, with notice, to avoid imputation (Rules 4-1.11 and 4-1.12)

Prospective clients: a lawyer who received disqualifying information from a prospective client is disqualified, but the firm may proceed if the lawyer took reasonable measures to limit what was learned, is timely screened and receives no part of the fee, and written notice is promptly given to the prospective client (Rule 4-1.18)
Imputed conflicts can be waived by the affected client's informed consent
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 1.10(a)(2) lets a firm avoid imputation of a lateral lawyer's former-client conflict by timely screening and notice. Florida's rule instead asks whether the lateral actually acquired material confidential information; do not assume screening alone cures a lateral's conflict in Florida.

topics.title: Advocacy and advertising
topics.intro: The advocacy rules (Subchapter 4-3 and 4-4) mostly track the Model Rules, but Florida still forbids threatening criminal or disciplinary charges to gain an advantage in a civil matter and restricts post-verdict contact with jurors. Florida's advertising rules (Subchapter 4-7) are among the most detailed in the country, including mandatory filing of many ads with the Bar and the 30-day waiting period for direct mail to accident victims.

rules.title: Candor toward the tribunal and client perjury
rules.rule: A lawyer may not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact previously made, fail to disclose directly adverse controlling authority not disclosed by opposing counsel, or offer evidence the lawyer knows is false. If the lawyer, the client or a witness the lawyer called has offered material evidence the lawyer later learns is false, the lawyer must take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal, even if the information is otherwise confidential; under Florida's rule these duties continue beyond the conclusion of the proceeding.
elements: First, remonstrate privately with the client and urge correction
If that fails, seek to withdraw if withdrawal will remedy the problem
If necessary, disclose to the tribunal
exceptions: A criminal defendant's right to testify does not let the lawyer present testimony the lawyer knows is false; Florida's rule states that a lawyer may not offer known false testimony in narrative form unless the tribunal orders it
A lawyer may refuse to offer evidence (other than a criminal defendant's own testimony) that the lawyer reasonably believes is false
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 3.3(c) ends the candor duties at the conclusion of the proceeding. Florida's Rule 4-3.3(d) says they continue beyond the conclusion of the proceeding and apply even if compliance requires revealing information otherwise protected by Rule 4-1.6. Florida also adds that a lawyer may not present known false testimony in narrative form unless the tribunal orders it.
rules.trap: 'Knows' means actual knowledge, which may be inferred from circumstances; a mere suspicion that the client is lying does not trigger the remedial duty.

rules.title: Fairness to the opposing party and the ban on threats
rules.rule: A lawyer may not unlawfully obstruct access to evidence or alter, destroy or conceal material with potential evidentiary value, fabricate evidence or assist a witness to testify falsely, or pay a witness contingent on the content of testimony or the outcome. A Florida lawyer also may not present, participate in presenting, or threaten to present criminal charges, or disciplinary charges under the Bar rules, solely to obtain an advantage in a civil matter.
exceptions: A lawyer may pay a witness's reasonable expenses and reasonable compensation for lost time, and an expert's reasonable fee that is not contingent on the outcome
rules.trap: Telling a debtor 'pay my client or I'll report you to the State Attorney' is a violation in Florida even if the criminal complaint would be well founded.
rules.split: The ABA Model Rules contain no counterpart to the old Code's ban on threatening criminal prosecution; ABA Formal Op. 92-363 permits such a threat if related to the civil claim and well founded. Florida's Rule 4-3.4 retains the prohibition and extends it to threats of Bar grievances.

rules.title: Ex parte contacts, jurors and trial publicity
rules.rule: A lawyer may not seek to influence a judge, juror or prospective juror by improper means or communicate ex parte with the judge about the merits of a pending case except as permitted by law or court order. After the jury is discharged, a Florida lawyer may not initiate contact with a juror about the trial except to determine whether the verdict may be subject to legal challenge, and then only if the lawyer has reason to believe grounds for a challenge may exist and first files a notice of intent to interview, with a copy to the trial judge and opposing counsel.
rules.tip: Extrajudicial statements are prohibited when the lawyer knows or reasonably should know they will be publicly disseminated and have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the proceeding (Rule 4-3.6).
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 3.5(c) generally allows post-discharge communication with jurors unless prohibited by law or court order, the juror does not want to talk, or the communication involves coercion or harassment. Florida's restriction is much tighter.

rules.title: Dealing with represented and unrepresented persons
rules.rule: In representing a client, a lawyer may not communicate about the subject of the representation with a person the lawyer knows to be represented by another lawyer in the matter, unless that lawyer consents or the communication is authorized by law or court order. With an unrepresented person, a lawyer may not state or imply disinterest, must correct any misunderstanding about the lawyer's role, and may not give legal advice other than advice to secure counsel when the person's interests conflict with the client's.
exceptions: Florida permits direct contact with a represented adverse party when a court rule, statute or contract requires notice or service directly on that party, limited to what is required, with a copy to the party's lawyer
The parties themselves may communicate directly with each other
rules.trap: The no-contact rule applies even if the represented person starts the conversation or consents; only the person's lawyer can consent.

rules.title: Advertising content: required and prohibited
rules.rule: A lawyer advertisement must include the name of at least one lawyer or the firm responsible for its content and the city or town of one or more bona fide offices. It may not contain a material misrepresentation of fact or law or be deceptive or inherently misleading, for example by promising results, referring to past results that are not objectively verifiable, making comparisons or characterizations of quality that cannot be objectively verified, or claiming board certification the lawyer does not hold.
elements: Testimonials are allowed only if the person giving them has had the actual experience described, is qualified to evaluate it, is not paid for it, the experience is representative, and the ad discloses that the viewer may not obtain the same or similar results
If the lawyer will refer the case to another lawyer, the ad must say so
Unduly manipulative or intrusive content is prohibited
rules.tip: Florida applies the advertising rules to websites and social media, although many of those are exempt from the filing requirement.

rules.title: Direct solicitation
rules.rule: A lawyer may not solicit professional employment, personally or through anyone acting on the lawyer's behalf, from a prospective client with whom the lawyer has no family or prior professional relationship, in person or otherwise, when a significant motive is pecuniary gain. 'Solicit' includes in-person contact, telephone calls and real-time electronic contact such as video calls, and any communication directed to a specific recipient that does not satisfy the written-communication and advertising rules. A lawyer may not charge or collect a fee for employment obtained in violation of this rule.
exceptions: Contact with family members, current or former clients, and people with whom the lawyer has a prior professional relationship
Contact without a pecuniary motive, such as pro bono outreach
rules.trap: Sending a paralegal or 'case runner' to a hospital to sign up accident victims is solicitation by the lawyer; so is paying anyone for recommending the lawyer.

rules.title: Written communications to prospective clients and the 30-day rule
rules.rule: A lawyer may not send a written communication directly to a prospective client seeking employment concerning a personal injury or wrongful death claim, or otherwise relating to an accident or disaster involving the recipient or a relative, unless the accident or disaster occurred more than 30 days before the mailing. Permitted targeted letters must, among other things, be plainly marked as an advertisement, begin with a statement that a recipient who has already retained a lawyer should disregard the letter, disclose how the lawyer learned of the matter, and be filed with the Bar.
exceptions: No targeted letter may be sent if the lawyer knows the person is represented in the matter, the person has said he or she does not want such communications, the communication involves coercion, duress or harassment, or the person's physical, emotional or mental state makes reasonable judgment unlikely
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 7.3 bans only live person-to-person solicitation, so targeted letters to accident victims are permitted at any time (unless the recipient has asked not to be contacted or the letter involves coercion, duress or harassment), with no waiting period, labeling or filing requirement. Florida's 30-day moratorium was upheld in Florida Bar v. Went For It, Inc.
rules.authority: R. Regulating Fla. Bar 4-7.18(b); Florida Bar v. Went For It, Inc., 515 U.S. 618 (1995)

rules.title: Filing advertisements with the Bar
rules.rule: Unless an exemption applies, a lawyer must file advertisements with The Florida Bar's ethics and advertising staff for review, along with the required fee. Exempt items include advertisements that contain only the presumptively valid information listed in the rules (such as the lawyer's name, contact information, areas of practice and bar admissions), and lawyer websites, which must still comply with the content rules.
rules.trap: Exemption from filing is not exemption from the substantive rules; an unfiled website that touts unverifiable results still violates Rule 4-7.13.
rules.split: The ABA Model Rules have no pre-dissemination filing or review requirement; Florida's filing regime is a distinctive feature tested on Part A.

topics.title: Misconduct, discipline and the practice of law
topics.intro: The Florida Supreme Court has exclusive constitutional authority over admission and discipline of lawyers, and The Florida Bar acts as its arm. This topic covers the catch-all misconduct rule (which has several Florida-only subsections), the duty to report other lawyers, the disciplinary process and sanctions, unlicensed practice, supervision of lawyers and staff, professional independence, and pro bono service.

rules.title: Professional misconduct under Rule 4-8.4
rules.rule: It is misconduct to violate the Rules (or knowingly assist or induce another to do so, or do so through another's acts), to commit a criminal act reflecting adversely on honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a lawyer, to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation, or to engage in conduct in connection with the practice of law that is prejudicial to the administration of justice. Florida's prejudice-to-justice provision expressly includes knowingly, or through callous indifference, disparaging, humiliating or discriminating against litigants, jurors, witnesses, court personnel or other lawyers on any basis, such as race, ethnicity, gender, religion, national origin, disability, marital status, sexual orientation, age, socioeconomic status, employment or physical characteristic.
elements: Florida-specific: failing to respond in writing to an official inquiry by bar counsel or a disciplinary agency when bar counsel or the agency is conducting an investigation
Florida-specific: willfully refusing, as determined by a court, to timely pay a child support obligation
Florida-specific: sexual conduct with a client that exploits or adversely affects the client or the relationship
rules.split: Florida did not adopt ABA Model Rule 8.4(g)'s free-standing harassment and discrimination provision; its anti-discrimination language is tied to conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice in connection with the practice of law.
rules.trap: A crime need not be a felony or related to law practice to be misconduct, but it must reflect on honesty, trustworthiness or fitness; conversely, dishonest conduct is misconduct even if it is not a crime.

rules.title: Candor in admission and disciplinary matters
rules.rule: An applicant for admission, or a lawyer in connection with an admission application or a disciplinary matter, may not knowingly make a false statement of material fact, or fail to disclose a fact necessary to correct a misapprehension known to have arisen, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority. Admission is handled by the Florida Board of Bar Examiners, which investigates each applicant's character and fitness.
exceptions: The rule does not require disclosure of information protected by the confidentiality rule
rules.trap: Concealing a past arrest or a debt default on the bar application is often treated more seriously than the underlying conduct; candor is itself the character test.
rules.authority: R. Regulating Fla. Bar 4-8.1; Art. V, § 15, Fla. Const.

rules.title: Duty to report another lawyer or a judge
rules.rule: A lawyer who knows that another lawyer has committed a violation of the Rules that raises a substantial question as to that lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a lawyer must inform the appropriate professional authority, and the same duty applies to a judge's violation of the judicial conduct rules that raises a substantial question as to the judge's fitness for office.
exceptions: No report is required if it would reveal information protected by the confidentiality rule
Information a lawyer gains while participating in an approved lawyers' assistance program is not subject to the reporting duty
rules.trap: The duty is triggered by knowledge of a serious violation, not by every rule breach or by mere rumor.

rules.title: The disciplinary process and sanctions
rules.rule: The Florida Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to regulate admission and discipline, and The Florida Bar investigates complaints as its agent. Bar counsel investigates; a grievance committee decides whether probable cause exists; if it does, the Bar files a formal complaint in the Supreme Court, which appoints a referee (a judge) to hear the case and recommend findings and discipline; the Supreme Court then reviews and enters the final judgment.
elements: Sanctions include admonishment, probation, public reprimand, suspension, disbarment and disciplinary revocation, and may be accompanied by restitution and costs
A suspension of more than 90 days requires proof of rehabilitation and a reinstatement proceeding; a suspension of 90 days or less ordinarily ends without one
A disbarred lawyer generally may not seek readmission for five years, unless the court orders a longer period or permanent disbarment
Emergency suspension is available when a lawyer appears to be causing great public harm, such as misappropriating trust funds
rules.authority: Art. V, § 15, Fla. Const.; R. Regulating Fla. Bar ch. 3 (incl. 3-5.1)

rules.title: Unlicensed practice and multijurisdictional practice
rules.rule: A lawyer may not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of its regulation of the legal profession or assist another in doing so. A lawyer admitted elsewhere may not establish an office or a systematic and continuous presence in Florida or hold out as admitted here, but may provide temporary services in limited situations, such as in association with an active Florida lawyer, under pro hac vice admission, or in matters reasonably related to the lawyer's home-state practice.
elements: Under Florida law, the unlicensed practice of law is a crime (a third-degree felony) as well as a matter for injunctive relief by the Florida Supreme Court
A lawyer may delegate work to nonlawyers but must supervise it and retain responsibility; nonlawyers may not give legal advice or set fees
rules.trap: A suspended or disbarred Florida lawyer who gives legal advice is engaged in unlicensed practice, and a lawyer who employs a suspended lawyer in a client-contact role risks assisting it.
rules.authority: R. Regulating Fla. Bar 4-5.5; Fla. Stat. § 454.23

rules.title: Supervising lawyers and nonlawyer assistants
rules.rule: Partners and lawyers with managerial authority must make reasonable efforts to ensure the firm has measures giving reasonable assurance that all lawyers and nonlawyer assistants conform to the Rules, and a lawyer with direct supervisory authority must make reasonable efforts to ensure the supervised person complies. A lawyer is responsible for another's violation if the lawyer orders or ratifies it, or knows of it when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated and fails to take reasonable remedial action.
exceptions: A subordinate lawyer does not violate the Rules by acting in accordance with a supervisor's reasonable resolution of an arguable question of professional duty

rules.title: Professional independence: no fee sharing with nonlawyers
rules.rule: A lawyer or firm may not share legal fees with a nonlawyer, form a partnership with a nonlawyer if any of its activities consist of the practice of law, or practice in a for-profit entity in which a nonlawyer owns an interest or directs the lawyer's professional judgment. A person who pays the lawyer to represent someone else may not direct or regulate the lawyer's professional judgment.
exceptions: Payments to a deceased lawyer's estate under an agreement, and the purchase price of a law practice sold under the rules
Including nonlawyer employees in a qualified pension, profit-sharing or retirement plan

Paying nonlawyer employees bonuses for work performed, including extraordinary effort on a particular case or over a period, but never a bonus based on cases or clients the employee brings to the firm
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 5.4(a)(3) lets nonlawyer employees share in any compensation or retirement plan based on profits. Florida's Rule 4-5.4(a) instead allows qualified pension, profit-sharing and retirement plans and work-based bonuses, and expressly forbids bonuses based on cases or clients the nonlawyer brings in.
rules.trap: Paying a paralegal a bonus of 10 percent of the fee in each case the paralegal brings in is both fee sharing with a nonlawyer and payment for recommending the lawyer.

rules.title: Pro bono public service
rules.rule: Each Florida Bar member in good standing should, as part of the member's professional responsibility, render pro bono legal services to the poor; the rule's aspirational goal is at least 20 hours a year or, alternatively, a contribution of $350 to a legal aid organization.
rules.split: ABA Model Rule 6.1 sets an aspirational 50 hours per year and has no reporting requirement; Florida's goal is 20 hours or $350, and every member must report annually.
rules.trap: Pro bono service is aspirational, not mandatory; failing to meet the goal is not by itself a disciplinary violation. What is mandatory is the annual report, on the dues statement, of whether the member met the goal.
